title: The One With All The Cheesecakes

jokes.text: Rachel's initial reluctance to try cheesecake followed by her immediate, ecstatic reversal upon tasting it
jokes.setup: Rachel says 'I'm not that much of a sweet tooth' — establishing herself as someone who would resist the cheesecake
jokes.punchline: She immediately groans in pleasure and declares it the best cheesecake she's ever had, completely abandoning her stated position
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection setup — she says one thing, does the opposite immediately. Well-paced and functional opener that establishes the cheesecake's power. Not particularly original but competently executed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No thanks, I'm not really into sweets.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh come on, just try a bite.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Mmm... oh my God. Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What did I tell you?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: This is the best thing I've ever tasted in my entire life!

jokes.text: Rachel gasps and calls Chandler a 'Thief' after learning the cheesecake was addressed to Mrs. Braverman downstairs
jokes.setup: Chandler discovers the cheesecake was delivered to the wrong address — it belongs to their neighbor
jokes.punchline: Rachel's single dramatic 'Thief' — delivered with outrage despite having just happily eaten the stolen cheesecake
jokes.explanation: The single word 'Thief' is beautifully economical. The irony is sharp — she ate it too, so the moral indignation is entirely hypocritical. The gasped delivery elevates it. Economy score is high because one word does enormous comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God! This is stolen cheesecake?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It fell off a truck.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A truck?! Chandler, we're eating stolen cheesecake!

jokes.text: Chandler's rationalization: 'Mrs. Braverman is gonna send away for a free one. And that way, we all win. The only losers are the big cheesecake conglomerate: Mama's Little Bakery.'
jokes.setup: Rachel correctly identifies that Chandler stole the cheesecake and that it is wrong
jokes.punchline: Chandler constructs an elaborate moral justification culminating in describing a small home-style bakery called 'Mama's Little Bakery' as a 'big cheesecake conglomerate'
jokes.explanation: This is classic Chandler — the elaborate self-serving rationalization that spirals into absurdity. The specific name 'Mama's Little Bakery' as the 'big cheesecake conglomerate' is the perfect deflating punchline. Very character-specific: only Chandler would construct this exact logic trap. The structure builds well through the rationalization before landing on the absurd reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because I already ate half of it.

jokes.text: Rachel's self-flagellation: 'I feel terrible. I'm a horrible, horrible, horrible person.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has just finished eating the entire stolen cheesecake and voiced moral objections
jokes.punchline: Despite having eaten just as much cheesecake as Chandler, she now proclaims herself 'a horrible, horrible, horrible person' with theatrical self-pity
jokes.explanation: The triple repetition of 'horrible' is a good comedic instinct — escalating self-condemnation is funny — but it's fairly predictable. Works within the cheesecake storyline's moral hypocrisy throughline.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Look, it's not stealing if it's from a big conglomerate. It's like... taking back from the man, you know?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Chandler, that's a bakery.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A small family bakery.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: Chandler's baffled 'Well, I'm sorry, what?' reaction to Rachel's self-condemnation
jokes.setup: Rachel has just declared herself 'a horrible, horrible, horrible person' over eating a cheesecake
jokes.punchline: Chandler's flat, confused response deflates her drama completely — he has no idea how to respond to that level of self-flagellation over a dessert
jokes.explanation: Solid straight-man reaction beat. The economy is excellent — four words that puncture Rachel's overwrought moral crisis. Chandler-as-straight-man works here even though it inverts his usual role.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can't believe I stole that cheesecake. I'm a terrible person. How could I do this? This isn't who I am!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Uh-huh. Yeah. Mmm-hmm.

jokes.text: Joey's soap opera coma plot: 'You know how I'm in a coma? Today they do a test on me and it turns out I'm not brain-dead.'
jokes.setup: Joey mentions he has a big day at work, suggesting something professionally significant
jokes.punchline: His 'big day' is that his comatose soap opera character is discovered to not be brain-dead — an absurdly specific, self-important revelation about a fictional TV character
jokes.explanation: Very Joey-specific — his earnest pride about a soap opera coma plotline is entirely in character. The character integration is strong because only Joey would treat 'my character isn't brain-dead' as a major career milestone to announce at breakfast.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey! My character on Days of Our Lives isn't brain-dead anymore!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh thank God. For a second there I was worried about you.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, my character! Dr. Drake Ramoray!

jokes.text: Joey's correction: 'Ah-ah, Mr. Smarty-Pants. It's just my character that's not brain-dead.'
jokes.setup: Joey announces his soap opera character is 'not brain-dead' as exciting news
jokes.punchline: Joey pre-emptively corrects an unspoken implication — clarifying his character isn't brain-dead, implying he's aware of what people might think about him personally
jokes.explanation: Smart self-awareness joke that plays on Joey's established reputation for not being bright. 'Mr. Smarty-Pants' as self-applied sarcasm is a funny touch. He's defending against an accusation nobody even made yet — which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So you're going to dinner with Joey?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, why?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, nothing. It's just that last week he told me all about your dating life, and the week before that he told me about Monica's cleaning obsession.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He what?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, you guys think you're so careful, but Joey tells me everything. We gossip about all of you.

jokes.text: Phoebe reveals she and Joey have secret monthly dinners to discuss the rest of the group: 'We get together about once a month to discuss the rest of you guys.'
jokes.setup: Ross asks what dinner plans Phoebe and Joey have. She answers straightforwardly.
jokes.punchline: The 'discussion' dinner exists, implying the group regularly sits in judgment of each other behind their backs — made funnier by Phoebe's total lack of embarrassment about it
jokes.explanation: A nice piece of world-building comedy. The idea that Phoebe and Joey have a formal monthly meeting to gossip about their friends is both absurd and entirely believable for these characters. Delivered with Phoebe's characteristic breezy candor, it's funnier for being stated so matter-of-factly.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, you guys were just talking about me?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, we were saying how you're really smart and funny and... generous.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, thank you. You know, Phoebe, you're... you're really talented. Your songs are... they're very unique.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Thanks.

jokes.text: Ross's desperate pivot after learning about the gossip dinners: 'May I say how lovely you look today?'
jokes.setup: Ross learns that Phoebe and Joey have monthly dinners specifically to discuss the friend group
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately tries to butter Phoebe up with an awkward compliment — transparently afraid of what they say about him
jokes.explanation: Perfectly timed character beat. Ross's anxiety and desire to be liked come through in one clumsy sentence. The speed of his pivot — no pause, just immediate damage control — is what makes it land. Very Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, you're not seven anymore, Monica.

jokes.text: Phoebe's flat 'Duly noted' in response to Ross's compliment
jokes.setup: Ross tries to butter Phoebe up with 'May I say how lovely you look today?'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's completely flat 'Duly noted' — acknowledging the compliment while making clear she sees exactly through what he's doing
jokes.explanation: Two words that do everything. 'Duly noted' is an unexpectedly formal register for Phoebe — the bureaucratic language in her mouth is inherently funny — and it perfectly signals that she's not falling for his flattery. Excellent economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You have to call him! You have to tell him that we want him at the wedding!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, I can't just call him out of the blue.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why not? What's the worst that could happen?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, there was that thing when we were kids...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What thing?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know, that time with the... and then in the garage...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God. How bad was it?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Let's just say he's probably going to show up at our wedding and object.

jokes.text: Ross's wounded reaction to discovering he wasn't invited to Cousin Frannie's wedding: 'I mean, from the ages of 7 to 9, Frannie and I were inseparable.'
jokes.setup: Ross is upset to learn he wasn't invited to his cousin's wedding while Monica was
jokes.punchline: His defense of their relationship is that they were 'inseparable' for a grand total of two years, in childhood — the specificity of '7 to 9' makes it funnier and sadder
jokes.explanation: The hyper-specific ages ('7 to 9') are the comedic choice that elevates this above a straight complaint. It implies the relationship completely collapsed by age 10, making his indignation absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, we all did weird things as kids.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I used to put on my mother's makeup and dance around the apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I collected giraffes.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's... actually kind of normal.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Ceramic giraffes. Like, two hundred of them.

jokes.text: Monica's dry dismissal: 'Well, maybe since the age of 9, Frannie's made some new friends.'
jokes.setup: Ross claims he and Frannie were 'inseparable' from ages 7 to 9 as justification for being upset about not being invited
jokes.punchline: Monica points out that in the intervening decades, Frannie may have moved on — delivered with perfect deadpan condescension
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-structured comeback. Monica-as-deadpan-deflater of Ross's ego is a perfect sibling dynamic. The phrase 'made some new friends' is deliciously condescending without being cruel. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, Joey left a note? What did it say?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It just says 'Can't make it. Big Daddy.'

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Big Daddy? Who's Big Daddy?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's me! That's my signature!

jokes.text: Ross reveals: 'her precious little Frannie tried to undress me several times, okay? If I hadn't stopped her, there probably wouldn't be a wedding to go to.'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to convince Monica to call their aunt and argue that his invitation was lost in the mail
jokes.punchline: Ross's lobbying argument is that Frannie repeatedly tried to undress him as children — a deeply weird revelation deployed as a reason he *deserves* to be at the wedding
jokes.explanation: Genuinely surprising dark reveal. The logic that he 'stopped her' and therefore 'there probably wouldn't be a wedding' is funny twisted reasoning. The escalation from 'I want to be invited' to 'my cousin tried to undress me' is an unexpected gear shift. Dark but played for maximum absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey, remember when you guys used to call me Big Daddy?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I don't think that ever happened.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, it should have. Big Daddy. That's a good nickname.

jokes.text: Monica's quiet admission: 'She tried to undress me too.' / 'I used to undress my cousin Glenn.'
jokes.setup: Ross reveals the shocking information that Frannie repeatedly tried to undress him as children
jokes.punchline: Monica casually admits it happened to her too, then Joey tops it by confessing HE was the one doing the undressing to his cousin — escalating depravity with each revelation
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat escalation. Monica's admission ('she tried to undress me too') is already funny as a matter-of-fact confirmation, but Joey's flip — where he's the perpetrator, not the victim, delivered with his characteristic breezy shamelessness — is an excellent topper. The structure is tight: setup, escalation, inversion. Joey's 'I used to undress my cousin Glenn' belongs in a highlights reel for its pure audacity.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Joseph Francis Tribbiani!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? What'd I do?

jokes.text: Joey's note signed 'Big Daddy' as his attempted nickname
jokes.setup: Phoebe reads a note Joey left canceling their plans
jokes.punchline: The note is signed 'Big Daddy' — a nickname Joey has apparently been trying to establish for himself, which is both grandiose and ridiculous
jokes.explanation: The note signing 'Big Daddy' is very Joey — his self-aggrandizement is always endearing. It sets up the running nickname gag. Character-specific and funny in context.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Look, there's a rule, okay? If a supermodel asks you out, you gotta go. It doesn't matter what you had planned.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, that's a good rule.

jokes.text: Ross introduces his failed nickname: 'Hey, you know what nickname never caught on? The Ross-a-tron.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is reacting to Joey's 'Big Daddy' nickname attempt
jokes.punchline: Ross volunteers that he too tried to establish a nickname — 'The Ross-a-tron' — and failed, with zero self-awareness about how terrible the nickname is
jokes.explanation: 'The Ross-a-tron' is a genuinely inspired piece of comedy writing. The name itself is catastrophically uncool — the '-tron' suffix aspirationally gestures at being robotic/powerful while sounding hopelessly dorky. The fact that Ross brings it up unprompted, admitting it 'never caught on' with no apparent embarrassment, is perfect character comedy. High quotability — it's the kind of line that becomes shorthand in fan culture.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Look, I'm really sorry I canceled on you guys. Let me make it up to you—dinner's on me!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'll pay for my own meal.

jokes.text: Joey states the rule: 'You can cancel plans with friends if there's a possibility for sex.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is upset that Joey canceled their plans for a date
jokes.punchline: Joey confidently declares this is 'the rule' — presenting a purely selfish social code as if it's established etiquette
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Joey — his confidence and lack of shame elevate what could be a crude observation into a character moment. The delivery of 'that is the rule' (from Ross) as corroboration makes it funnier. Very character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey, you know what? People have been calling me 'The Rossatron' all week.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, they haven't.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, they will be. I'm working it into casual conversation. Like, 'Hey, the Rossatron needs another coffee,' or 'The Rossatron is going to the movies.'

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, that's not how nicknames work.

jokes.text: Ross immediately backs Joey up: 'Phoebe, he's right. That is the rule.'
jokes.setup: Joey has just stated his self-serving 'rule' about canceling plans for sex
jokes.punchline: Ross — who is currently alone and dateless — immediately and earnestly confirms Joey's bro-code rule as if it's established fact
jokes.explanation: Ross's instant agreement is funny because it's so nakedly his desire to be cool and to side with the men. The irony that he's the least likely beneficiary of this rule makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, so are we using the nickname or not?

jokes.text: Joey's apology offer: 'How about dinner tomorrow night? I'll pay for myself.'
jokes.setup: Joey is apologizing to Phoebe for ditching her and trying to make it up to her
jokes.punchline: His grand gesture of making amends is offering to pay for his own dinner — the bar is set comically low
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Joey — his idea of a generous concession is meeting the minimum social expectation that everyone pays for their own meal. The gap between what an apology 'gesture' should be and what he's actually offering is delightful. Character integration is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I forgot what cheesecake tastes like.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, it's like... it's like nothing. It's like air.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It tastes like air?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, like really good air.

jokes.text: Ross calls across the room: 'Joe, while you're over there, how about another beer for The Ross-a-tron?'
jokes.setup: Earlier Ross mentioned 'The Ross-a-tron' was a nickname that never caught on
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately tries to use the failed nickname in casual conversation, completely undermining his own acknowledgment that it never worked
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback execution. Ross introducing 'The Ross-a-tron' as a failed nickname and then immediately trying to use it anyway is perfectly character-consistent — his obliviousness and desperate desire to be cool collide. The callback elevates both jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It was just fine.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: The way that creamy filling just melts on your tongue, and the graham cracker crust shatters delicately between your teeth, releasing those buttery notes that dance across your palate...

jokes.text: Joey's confused 'Ross...' — a half-question, half-wince reaction to hearing 'The Ross-a-tron'
jokes.setup: Ross has just deployed 'The Ross-a-tron' in live conversation
jokes.punchline: Joey's baffled, trailing 'Ross...' — not even a complete sentence, just bewilderment — followed by the almost wistful 'Is that back?' confirms the nickname is as bad as it sounds
jokes.explanation: Joey's minimal-word reaction is funnier than a full sentence would be. The unfinished 'Ross...' conveys volumes. 'Is that back?' implies it was attempted and retired before — adding depth to Ross's failed nickname history.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I have to say something. That description was so sensual, I think I need a cigarette... and I don't even smoke anymore.

jokes.text: Chandler about the second cheesecake: 'I can't seem to say goodbye.'
jokes.setup: A second cheesecake has arrived, also misaddressed. Rachel tells Chandler to just bring it downstairs.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's admission that he 'can't seem to say goodbye' to a cheesecake treats his dessert obsession with the gravity of a romantic relationship
jokes.explanation: The romantic/emotional language applied to cheesecake is a consistent comedic register in this storyline and it works here. 'Can't seem to say goodbye' is a lovely, economical line.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: We are not going to think about cheesecake. We are just going to sit here and have a normal conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: OK, what do you want to talk about?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't know... um... the big salad.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The big salad? Rachel, that's not going to work.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? I say we just go to the source. We go to Chicago, we go to the bakery where they make it, and we just get a whole cheesecake.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Chandler, that's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Is it? Is it really?

jokes.text: Chandler's sensory rhapsody about the cheesecake: 'It had a buttery, crumbly, graham-cracker crust... with a very rich... yet light cream-cheese filling.'
jokes.setup: Rachel dismisses the cheesecake as 'fine,' trying to be the voice of reason
jokes.punchline: Chandler launches into an increasingly reverent, almost romantic description of the cheesecake's texture and layers, speaking about it like a lost lover
jokes.explanation: The deliberate, loving pace of his description — with pauses for reverence — plays well. The joke is the contrast between Rachel's dismissive 'it was fine' and Chandler's near-religious experience. Good sustained comic character work.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Mel Tormé died?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, that was like three years ago.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Why didn't anybody tell me?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It was on the news, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, I don't watch the news! I watch sports center. And occasionally, Cops.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, what date is this paper from?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Three years ago.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh man! There's a sale at the Gap!

jokes.text: Rachel's involuntary response: 'Wow, my whole mouth just filled with saliva.'
jokes.setup: Rachel was trying to be the responsible one who resists the cheesecake temptation; Chandler has just described it rhapsodically
jokes.punchline: Despite herself, Rachel's body betrays her — her salivating admission is both gross and deeply human, and completely undermines her moral high ground
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny line — specific, physical, honest, and perfectly timed. 'My whole mouth just filled with saliva' is the kind of oversharing TMI confession that is funnier for being involuntary. The specificity ('whole mouth') elevates it above a vague reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: There is no excuse for not having enough seating!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, back when you were big, you took up two chairs anyway.

jokes.text: Chandler, asked where he wants to go for lunch, says: 'Mama's Little Bakery, Chicago, Illinois.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has talked them both into going out for lunch instead of stealing the cheesecake again, suggesting they 'just go eat'
jokes.punchline: When asked where he wants to go, Chandler names the cheesecake company — full name, city, state — revealing that the 'lunch' detour was never going to work
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is near-perfect: Rachel delivers a sensible plan (let's go eat lunch), asks where he wants to go — a totally reasonable question — and Chandler's answer of 'Mama's Little Bakery, Chicago, Illinois' perfectly demolishes the entire premise. The specificity of 'Chicago, Illinois' (as if he's already looked up the address) is an inspired detail. It's economical, character-perfect, and gets a big laugh. This is what a well-executed callback looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She has a very broad back.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You mean wide?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, broad.

jokes.text: Joey reacts to an old newspaper: 'Aw. Mel Tormé died.'
jokes.setup: Joey is reading what turns out to be an old newspaper
jokes.punchline: Joey is saddened by Mel Tormé's death — which happened a year ago — having just now discovered it from a year-old paper
jokes.explanation: The joke has a nice delayed-reaction quality. Joey being a year behind the news is a solid character beat. Works as a lead-in to the Sam Goody's punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, Ross gets to bring someone? Who is he bringing?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? How is that fair? I've been single for months!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, so he just gets a plus-one because he's in a relationship for five minutes?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what, that's fine. That's FINE. I'm completely fine with this.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm not fine.

jokes.text: Joey's follow-up: 'Oh, does that mean the Sam Goody's sale is over?'
jokes.setup: Ross has told Joey that the newspaper is a year old, implying Mel Tormé's death was old news
jokes.punchline: Joey's concern immediately pivots from grief over a dead musician to whether a retail sale at Sam Goody's is still on — revealing his priorities
jokes.explanation: Excellent topper. The pivot from genuine sorrow about Mel Tormé to immediate mercenary concern about a CD store sale is a perfect Joey moment. The specific brand name 'Sam Goody's' adds period-perfect texture. This beats the setup joke significantly and earns the escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't cancel on Joan. She's a very important woman. We have plans.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You don't understand. Linguistics professors are wild. We're out till like 9, 9:30 sometimes.

jokes.text: Monica's response about why Frannie didn't know she'd only need one seat: 'Yeah, but she doesn't know that. I mean, the last time she saw you, you would've turned one of those little wedding chairs into kindling.'
jokes.setup: Monica reveals that Ross wasn't invited due to 'limited seating.' Ross objects that he is 'just one tiny person.'
jokes.punchline: Ross mockingly implies that at their last meeting, he had apparently been much heavier — suggesting Frannie's seating concern was based on a previous, heftier Ross
jokes.explanation: The 'kindling' image is vivid and mean in a fun sibling-rivalry way. Monica casually implying Ross was enormously fat at some point is a good dark aside. 'Turned those little chairs into kindling' is a nicely specific image.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Is that another cheesecake?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, technically it's not stealing if we're just borrowing it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's the definition of stealing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, no, we'll put it back before they even notice. Plus, they probably over-ordered anyway. We're actually helping them by reducing waste.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's... that's not how that works.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And think about it — they're a big company, they can afford the loss. But we're just two struggling people who deserve a little happiness. Cheesecake is basically a food group. The real crime would be letting it go to waste. Are you really going to let that happen? Don't you care about the environment?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, are you actually concerned about the environment right now?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm very concerned.

jokes.text: Ross describes his date Joan: 'And despite what some people say, not broad-backed.'
jokes.setup: Ross is describing his date Joan to Monica, listing her impressive attributes (assistant professor, tall, beautiful)
jokes.punchline: He adds the qualifier 'not broad-backed' — defensively addressing a criticism that someone has apparently made about Joan, which raises more questions than it answers
jokes.explanation: The specific detail 'not broad-backed' is an inspired comedy choice — the very act of defending against this accusation plants it in everyone's mind. The implication that multiple people have called Joan broad-backed, requiring a preemptive defense, is funnier than any direct description. Sets up the running 'broad-back' joke.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: David? David? David?

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Yes?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, his name really is David!

jokes.text: Monica's outrage: 'Wait a minute. You got Ross Geller and guest? I wasn't invited, and you got and guest?'
jokes.setup: Monica is already upset about not being invited. Ross reveals his invitation includes 'and guest.'
jokes.punchline: Monica's indignation escalates — not only was she excluded while Ross was included, but he gets a PLUS ONE she doesn't even get
jokes.explanation: The indignation is well-played Monica character work, escalating the insult naturally. The 'and guest' detail is a nice comic specificity. Fairly standard sitcom escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Did you get a haircut?

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: No, I got them all cut.

jokes.text: Chandler jumping in: 'I think the rule applies here. Since he has a chance to get on broad-back—' / Ross: 'Not broad-back!'
jokes.setup: 'Not broad-backed' was Ross's defensive disclaimer about Joan
jokes.punchline: Chandler uses 'broad-back' as shorthand in an argument about the rule, turning Ross's defensiveness into a nickname-level callback
jokes.explanation: Chandler weaponizes the 'broad-back' denial beautifully. Ross's frantic correction 'Not broad-back!' confirms the descriptor has already stuck. Good callback economy.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: It's Lenin. From certain angles.

jokes.text: Ross explains why the 'sex cancels plans' rule applies: 'I think the rule applies here. Since he has a chance to get on broad-back—' / 'Not broad-back!'
jokes.setup: Ross is explaining why the 'cancel plans for sex' rule applies to his situation with Joan
jokes.punchline: He casually references Joan as 'broad-back' mid-argument, triggering Ross's immediate and vehement correction — both continuing the running gag and showing how much it's gotten under his skin
jokes.explanation: The 'broad-back' callback works well — Monica using it casually, Ross's explosive denial is a good escalation of the running gag. His sensitivity about it confirms the joke. The pattern of 'casual use / outraged correction' is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't cancel on them. I never cancel on my friends. It's like, the one principle I have.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, except for that time I cancelled on Monica, and that time I cancelled on Rachel, and... okay, I cancel a lot. But I'm not canceling this time!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Pheebs, it's the love of your life.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what am I doing?! I'm canceling!

jokes.text: Ross explains why he wants to go to the wedding: 'Because... she's my cousin. I mean, we grew up together... Family, you know? And all that's important to me.' — then Monica agrees and Ross's immediate smug 'We'll see. Ha, ha.'
jokes.setup: Ross delivers a sincere-seeming speech about family and wanting to be at Frannie's wedding for the right reasons
jokes.punchline: The moment Monica gives in, Ross drops the warm family rhetoric and pivots to a smug, almost threatening 'We'll see. Ha, ha.' — revealing his true motivations (revenge, pettiness)
jokes.explanation: Beautiful character bait-and-switch. Ross's speech about family is entirely earnest in delivery — he's playing Monica — and the instant drop to 'We'll see. Ha, ha.' the moment she relents is a great reveal of his true intent. Very Ross — his petty vindictiveness masked as sentimentality. The structure is near-ideal.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I have to stick to my principles. I can't compromise.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What if we did it this way instead?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, okay!

jokes.text: Chandler and Rachel realize they forgot to pay for lunch: 'So apparently, we just don't pay for food anymore.'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Rachel have returned from their distraction-free lunch, congratulating themselves on avoiding the cheesecake
jokes.punchline: They discover neither paid — they were so distracted by their cheesecake obsession/moral crisis that they simply walked out of a restaurant without paying
jokes.explanation: Funny situational beat. The deadpan 'apparently we just don't pay for food anymore' is a good line — matter-of-fact in its admission of accidental crime. Reinforces the cheesecake obsession's ability to make them lose their minds.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What are you eating?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's tofu cake.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Tofu cake? That's disgusting!

jokes.text: The cheesecake is still sitting in the hallway — visual beat of both characters spotting it simultaneously
jokes.setup: They were supposed to drop the cheesecake at Mrs. Braverman's door. They got distracted by going to lunch.
jokes.punchline: The cheesecake is exactly where they left it, sitting in the hallway, like it's been waiting for them. Both react with something between guilt and longing.
jokes.explanation: Visual comedy beat — the cheesecake as recurring temptation object in the hallway is a nice physical comedy setup. The 'Huh! It's still there' line confirms they're both looking at it with the same guilty/hungry expression.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't go, I have to be somewhere else.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? Come on, Pheebs, you have to come!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I made other plans.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, un-make them! Joey Tribbiani does not accept cancellations.

jokes.text: Chandler's escalating rationalizations for taking the cheesecake: 'She could be out of town... By then the cheesecake may have gone bad... We don't want her to come back to bad cheesecake... That could kill her... Wouldn't want that... We're protecting her.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Braverman appears to be out, and the cheesecake is unattended in the hallway
jokes.punchline: Chandler constructs a chain of increasingly absurd logic — she's gone, it'll go bad, it'll kill her, they're actually heroes — until stealing the cheesecake is reframed as a humanitarian act
jokes.explanation: Another great Chandler rationalization sequence, echoing the 'Mama's Little Bakery conglomerate' logic from earlier. The escalation is well-structured — each step follows logically from the last, until the conclusion ('we're protecting her') is completely insane. The rhythm of 'That could kill her / Wouldn't want that / No, we're protecting her' is a nice comedic trio.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: She's my cousin! We share the same blood!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: The same blood runs through our veins!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We are connected by blood!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, Monica, I think people get it.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'But move quick. Why? I heard her moving around in there.' — panic-stealing the cheesecake
jokes.setup: They've convinced themselves to take the cheesecake as a 'protective' act
jokes.punchline: Chandler reveals he can hear Mrs. Braverman inside — meaning she's NOT out of town, completely demolishing his entire justification — and they panic-steal it anyway
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Mrs. Braverman is home — thus destroying the entire rationalization — and they still take it is a great escalation of their moral collapse. The 'go, go, go' panic adds physical energy to the comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more disappointed?

jokes.text: Phoebe's gasp at seeing David: 'Oh, my God, that's David... Oh, you say someone's name enough, they turn around.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe excitedly whispers David's name multiple times, and he turns around
jokes.punchline: Phoebe observes, with cheerful pseudo-wisdom, that repeatedly saying someone's name causes them to turn around — as if this is a profound discovery rather than basic human behavior
jokes.explanation: Very Phoebe — she states an obvious behavioral fact as if it's wisdom she's unlocking in real time. The delivery of this as a revelation is what makes it funny. 'Oh, you say someone's name enough, they turn around' is a charmingly dumb observation.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Before we eat, I think we should go around the table and share something really personal. Something we've never told anyone before.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Like, I'll start. When I was living on the street, I had an imaginary friend named Gluntz, and he was the only one who understood me.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Now come on, everyone. Don't you want to bond? This is important. This is what friendship is all about.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, and we should probably do this slowly. You know, really take our time so we can fully process everyone's feelings.

jokes.text: David describes a statue in Minsk that reminds him of Phoebe: 'There's a statue in Minsk that reminds me of you so much. I mean, it's actually of Lenin... but, you know, at certain angles...'
jokes.setup: David is saying romantic things about how much he thinks of Phoebe in Russia
jokes.punchline: The statue that reminds him of her turns out to be Lenin — a bald, bearded Soviet revolutionary — with the qualifier 'at certain angles,' which makes it both more absurd and funnier
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The setup is entirely romantic — he thinks of her constantly, there's a statue — and the punchline (Lenin) is a perfect absurdist reveal. 'At certain angles' is an inspired addition that transforms a surreal joke into a perfect one, implying he has actually stood around a Lenin statue at different angles to find the Phoebe resemblance. Originality and structure are both excellent. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She's like a scientist or something.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Really? What kind of scientist?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, she graduated high school.

jokes.text: Phoebe's self-reversal: 'No. No, no. If I don't have my principles, I don't have anything.' — then immediately: 'Or I should rush through dinner with Joey and I could meet David at 9.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just delivered a passionate speech about keeping her principles and not canceling on Joey
jokes.punchline: Without even a breath, she immediately proposes a compromise that completely undermines her principled stand — the reversal happens mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic reversal. The speed of it is key — she doesn't even let the inspiring speech land before dismantling it. This mirrors the Rachel cheesecake reversal at the top of the episode but lands harder because of Phoebe's earlier self-righteousness with Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, I have an impossible challenge for you. I want you to say something without moving your lips.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: mmph

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh wow, you did it!

jokes.text: Chandler eating the second cheesecake alone, then Rachel busting him: 'Are you eating the cheesecake without me?' / Chandler's muffled 'Mm-mm.'
jokes.setup: They agreed to bring the second cheesecake downstairs. Chandler has clearly started eating it without Rachel.
jokes.punchline: He's caught with his mouth full and denies it with an unconvincing 'Mm-mm' — the lie is physically impossible to sell given he's clearly eating
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy beat. The 'Mm-mm' denial while clearly eating is a timeless gag. Well-executed if not particularly original. Chandler's escalating moral collapse continues.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm gonna tell on you guys. You stole a cheesecake from the bakery and ate it in the hallway like a couple of common criminals!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Chandler, it's not that big of a deal.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Not that big of a deal? You two are like Bonnie and Clyde! Except instead of robbing banks, you're robbing delicious baked goods!

jokes.text: Rachel's disgusted reaction to the cheesecake being described as 'tofu cake' — she recoils with an 'Aah.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is eating the cheesecake in the hallway and tries to hide it from Rachel by calling it 'tofu cake'
jokes.punchline: Rachel's horrified 'Aah' at the mere mention of tofu cake is an instant rejection — she's not fooled, she's just repulsed by the alternative
jokes.explanation: Quick physical reaction beat. Rachel's recoil from 'tofu' as an obscene concept is a mild but effective laugh. Not deep comedy but serves the scene momentum well.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? Fine. You want the cheesecake? Take it. But I'm telling everyone that you said Monica's new haircut makes her look like a lesbian.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?! I would never say that!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know. That's what makes it so believable.

jokes.text: Monica introducing herself at the wedding: 'I'm a relative and I didn't get invited, okay? A blood relative. Blood.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Ross are greeting other guests at the reception
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately airs her grievance to a stranger, emphasizing 'blood' in an increasingly unhinged way
jokes.explanation: Monica's social collapse at the wedding is cringe comedy done well. The repetition of 'Blood.' at the end — after a pause — is a nice escalation. Very in character for Monica's competitive, aggrieved nature.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, here are the rules. No double-dipping, no eating from the middle, and absolutely no touching the other person's piece.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Got it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm serious, Rachel. This is serious cheesecake.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know, I know.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We clear?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Crystal clear.

jokes.text: Ross to Monica at the wedding: 'Stop saying blood to strangers.'
jokes.setup: Monica is ranting to wedding guests about being a blood relative who wasn't invited, repeatedly saying the word 'blood'
jokes.punchline: Ross's quiet, mortified intervention — not addressing the substance of her complaint, just the word 'blood' — is a perfect straight-man beat
jokes.explanation: Six words, perfectly chosen. Ross doesn't engage with whether her complaint is valid — he only objects to the word 'blood' being said to strangers, which is both funnier and more socially accurate. The specificity of 'to strangers' elevates it. High economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm taking my time with this cheesecake. I'm savoring every bite.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh no! My piece! It dropped in the hallway!

jokes.text: Ross to Monica: 'Stop saying blood to strangers.'
jokes.setup: Monica repeatedly says 'blood' to emphasize her kinship to a stranger at the wedding
jokes.punchline: Ross's flat correction is the button — it's the most reasonable sentence imaginable in this context
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that do exactly what's needed. The normalcy of the correction against the absurdity of the situation is the joke. 'Stop saying blood to strangers' is oddly quotable because it's such a specific and reasonable piece of advice.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Aunt Millie, what are you doing?!

dialogue.speaker: Aunt Millie
dialogue.line: Oh honey, I'm so happy for you!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes, but why are you kissing me like that?

jokes.text: Monica's immediate assessment after the neighbor couple says they live next door to the happy couple: 'Okay, you're fine.'
jokes.setup: Monica has been interrogating wedding guests about how they know the bride and groom, implicitly ranking their right to be there while she wasn't invited
jokes.punchline: After getting an answer she considers satisfactory, Monica grants this stranger her explicit approval: 'Okay, you're fine.' — as if she's the bouncer
jokes.explanation: Very Monica — her compulsive need to rank, judge, and render verdicts even in social situations where she has no authority. 'Okay, you're fine' as a formal approval granted to a stranger at someone else's wedding is funny character work.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm gonna be so nice to her. I'm gonna be so nice, she's gonna wish she never met me.

jokes.text: Joey at the restaurant: 'This slow-roasted salmon... just how slow are we talking? It's already been roasted. Oh, then no. Maybe I should hear those specials again.'
jokes.setup: The waiter is taking orders. Phoebe orders quickly. Joey asks about an item on the menu.
jokes.punchline: Joey's question about how 'slow' the slow-roasted salmon is reveals he expected to watch it being roasted — and now that he knows it's pre-roasted, he wants to restart the specials process entirely
jokes.explanation: Excellent Joey food joke. The question 'just how slow are we talking?' implies he has strong opinions about roasting pace. The reveal that pre-roasting disqualifies it, requiring him to rehear all the specials, is perfect Joey logic — his relationship with food is so intense that menu items can be disqualified on procedural grounds.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What could I have possibly done?

dialogue.speaker: Frannie
dialogue.line: You slept with my husband!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That was before you were married to him!

jokes.text: Phoebe reciting the specials from memory — having heard them three times
jokes.setup: Joey asks to hear the specials again
jokes.punchline: Phoebe recites them from memory, having been forced to listen to them repeatedly — including 'a very special lobster ravioli'
jokes.explanation: Light gag — Phoebe's exasperation with Joey's indecision expressed through memorization. Works as a character beat more than a standalone joke. 'A very special lobster ravioli' is a mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Морская звезда светит в ночи, как твои глаза.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's so romantic! What did you say?

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: A starfish shines in the night like your eyes.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: A... starfish?

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: Yes, well, in Russian the word for starfish is very poetic. I couldn't think of the word for star.

jokes.text: Waiter: 'Actually, we're out of the lobster ravioli.' / Joey: 'Oh, well, that changes everything.'
jokes.setup: Joey has forced everyone to hear the specials multiple times. The lobster ravioli has been mentioned each time.
jokes.punchline: The waiter mentions they're out of lobster ravioli — and Joey treats this information as a complete overhaul of the dining landscape, requiring him to reconsider everything
jokes.explanation: Five words that capture Joey's food personality completely: 'Oh, well, that changes everything.' The gravity of the statement — appropriate for a business negotiation or a life decision — applied to a restaurant menu item is pitch-perfect. High character integration, high economy. This is exactly what an 8 on craft looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You could visit David in Russia!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't get a passport.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Because I'm not a real person. My birth certificate is a letter from my mother.

jokes.text: Joey's 'progress' at the restaurant: 'Yes. I will have the lobster ravioli.' — after they've been told it's unavailable
jokes.setup: Phoebe checks if he's made any progress on ordering. He's been deliberating for a very long time.
jokes.punchline: Joey has finally decided — on the item they were specifically told is not available. He's been deliberating for so long he's circled back to what was eliminated.
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback. After all that deliberation, all those specials, 'that changes everything' — Joey has arrived at the one thing he can't have. The structure is excellent: the entire ordering sequence has been building to this absurd conclusion. Character integration is high because only Joey would take this long and land on an impossible order.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I could do that! I'm great with science stuff.

jokes.text: Joey confronts Phoebe about her date: 'No, no, Pheebs, you must be mistaken... because you wouldn't schedule a date on the night you have plans with a friend.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has admitted she has a date tonight — the same night she made Joey feel guilty for canceling on her
jokes.punchline: Joey delivers her own principle back to her with exaggerated, mock-innocent confusion — a perfect mirror of her earlier speech
jokes.explanation: Joey's feigned innocent confusion — playing dumb when he's actually making a sharp point — is well-executed irony. The callback to Phoebe's principled speech is satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God, oh my God! No, no, no, no, no!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: There has to be one piece that didn't touch the floor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Five-second rule! Five-second rule!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: This one's still good, this one's still good... Oh, come on!

jokes.text: Joey defends his canceled date: 'She was a scientist too.' / Phoebe: 'She was?' / Joey: 'Well, she graduated high school.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe argues David is special because he's a scientist. Joey argues his date was also special.
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals that his date's scientific credential is having graduated high school — he's equating the two with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection with a sharp punchline. The setup (she was a scientist too) creates expectation of a parallel, then 'she graduated high school' demolishes any pretense while revealing Joey's completely innocent sincerity. The beat between 'She was a scientist too' and 'Well, she graduated high school' is a near-perfect joke structure. High marks across the board.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Hey Ross, Aunt Frannie's here!

dialogue.speaker: Aunt Frannie
dialogue.line: Ross! Come give your Aunt Frannie a kiss!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, uh, hey Aunt Frannie. How about a hug instead?

dialogue.speaker: Aunt Frannie
dialogue.line: Don't be silly!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, no — we can just hug, right? Just a regular hug?

dialogue.speaker: Aunt Frannie
dialogue.line: I haven't seen you in years!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, and it's great to see you, but — oh God, no, not the lips! Why is it always on the lips?!

jokes.text: Joey, still at the restaurant after Phoebe leaves: 'What are you still doing here? I told you, lobster ravioli.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has gotten up and left for her date. Joey is left at the table.
jokes.punchline: Joey is apparently still negotiating with the waiter about the unavailable lobster ravioli — he hasn't moved on and is now giving orders as if the waiter's job is to source it
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the lobster ravioli running gag. Joey hasn't been chasing Phoebe or processing the conversation — he's been locked in with the waiter about the impossible order. 'I told you, lobster ravioli' implies he's been repeating this throughout the entire Phoebe confrontation, as if the waiter just needs to try harder. Very high economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'I will give you $100 to whistle right now.' — Chandler is eating cheesecake with a full mouth
jokes.setup: Chandler has been caught eating the cheesecake solo and his mouth is full
jokes.punchline: Rachel's $100 whistling challenge highlights the physical impossibility of whistling with a mouth full of cheesecake — the specific dollar amount makes it funnier than a vague dare
jokes.explanation: Sharp, specific, and playful. '$100 to whistle' is a great comic proposition — the specific dollar amount signals Rachel is fully committed to this joke. The visual of Chandler unable to whistle while stuffed with cheesecake would play brilliantly. High economy score.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'What are you gonna do? Gonna run and tell Monica or Joey? No, you'd have to tell them what we did. We are dessert stealers. We are living outside the law.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has caught Chandler eating the cheesecake solo and is indignant
jokes.punchline: Chandler correctly identifies that Rachel can't report him without implicating herself, then dramatically declares them 'dessert stealers' living 'outside the law' — treating a cheesecake theft like a crime drama
jokes.explanation: 'We are dessert stealers. We are living outside the law.' is excellent — the melodrama applied to petty cheesecake theft, the crime-thriller register, and the logical observation that she can't report him all land together. 'Living outside the law' is a quotable, well-crafted line. High character integration because Chandler's verbal self-justification is his defining trait.

jokes.text: Chandler threatens to tell Monica that Rachel called her cheesecake 'dry and mealy' as leverage in the cheesecake split
jokes.setup: They are negotiating how to split the stolen cheesecake between them
jokes.punchline: Chandler deploys the nuclear option — threatening to tell Monica, an obsessive cook who would be devastated — that Rachel insulted her baking, using it as leverage in a dessert negotiation
jokes.explanation: Smart joke that ties together multiple character traits — Monica's cooking obsession, Rachel's insecurity about confrontation, and Chandler's manipulative streak. Using Monica as a threat weapon is very character-aware writing.

jokes.text: The extended cheesecake-splitting negotiation: 'Well, this side looks bigger' / 'But there's more crust on this side' / 'So maybe if I measure it...' / 'For God's sake, pick a piece!'
jokes.setup: They are literally dividing a stolen cheesecake into equal halves in a building hallway
jokes.punchline: The negotiation becomes so granular and petty — examining crust distribution, contemplating measurement — that it escalates into an absurd standoff before Rachel snaps
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe comedy. The pettiness of obsessing over crust distribution in a stolen cheesecake in a hallway is inherently funny. 'For God's sake, pick a piece!' is the perfect exasperated climax.

jokes.text: After all the agonizing, Chandler points out: 'So the smaller piece.'
jokes.setup: After an absurdly lengthy deliberation, Rachel has finally picked a half of the cheesecake
jokes.punchline: Chandler's flat observation that she picked the smaller piece — after all that — is a perfect deflating topper
jokes.explanation: Three words that perfectly puncture the entire agonizing negotiation. The economy here is exceptional — 'So the smaller piece' is funnier for how much effort it dismisses.

jokes.text: Chandler's exit speech: 'No sharing, no switching, and don't come crying to me if you eat your piece too fast.'
jokes.setup: They have split the cheesecake and are going their separate ways in the hallway
jokes.punchline: Chandler sets out rules with the gravity of a business contract, specifically anticipating that Rachel will eat hers too fast and want his — which is so specific it implies this has happened before or he knows exactly what she'll do
jokes.explanation: The specific warning about eating her piece 'too fast' is prophetic and funny — sets up the inevitable next beat. The formal contract language applied to stolen dessert continues the episode's comedic register.

jokes.text: Rachel immediately drops her piece of cheesecake on the floor — audible SHOUT then 'Oh!'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just delivered his 'no sharing, no switching' speech. Rachel has her half.
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately drops the cheesecake on the hallway floor — before she's even taken two steps — a perfect physical comedy payoff to the elaborate negotiation
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff. The elaborate negotiation, the formal rules, the gravity of the cheesecake split — all demolished instantly by Rachel dropping it immediately. The structure is excellent: the longer and more elaborate the setup, the funnier the sudden physical collapse. The [SHOUTS] indicates a full physical comedy beat. High structure score because this is textbook joke architecture.

jokes.text: The cheesecake falls on the hallway floor — both gasp in horror
jokes.setup: Chandler has just delivered his pompous 'no sharing, no switching' speech
jokes.punchline: The cheesecake immediately hits the floor — a slapstick puncturing of all their elaborate rules
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy escalation. The elaborate setup of rules and territorial cheesecake governance is instantly demolished by a dropped box. Timing-dependent — works best in performance — but structurally sound as a comedic beat.

jokes.text: Chandler's refusal to share after Rachel drops her piece: 'No switching, no sharing. And don't come crying to me.' / 'Ha, ha. I may just sit here and have my cake all day.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has dropped her cheesecake on the floor and is devastated
jokes.punchline: Chandler robotically repeats his own rules back at her and smugly settles in to eat his piece right there in the hallway, in front of her — an act of pure petty cruelty over cheesecake
jokes.explanation: The callback to his own rules lands well, and 'I may just sit here and have my cake all day' — sitting in the apartment hallway to eat a stolen dessert — is a great image. His smug relish elevates the pettiness to comic perfection.

jokes.text: Ross's repeated 'Why? Why on the lips?' reaction to Aunt Millie kissing him on the lips
jokes.setup: Ross greets his Aunt Millie at the wedding, and she kisses him on the lips
jokes.punchline: Ross's quiet, baffled 'Why? Why on the lips?' — asking the universe, not anyone in particular — is a perfectly observed family discomfort moment
jokes.explanation: Universally relatable family discomfort. The repeated 'why' — not addressed to anyone, just existential — is a good comedic instinct. 'Why on the lips?' is quotable and specific. Sets up its callback beautifully.

jokes.text: Monica's immediate, explosive response to learning it was Frannie who found and showed their parents Ross's Playboys: 'That bitch.'
jokes.setup: Ross is warning Monica to 'be nice' and not ambush Frannie at her own wedding
jokes.punchline: Monica's entire disposition changes the instant she hears this new information — dropping all her 'be civilized' pretense with an immediate, heartfelt 'That bitch.'
jokes.explanation: Two words, perfectly placed. Monica has just been lecturing Ross on being civil, and the revelation of the Playboys-and-parents incident causes an instant personality reversal. The deadpan absolute conviction of 'That bitch.' — no hedging, no escalation, just arrival — is excellent economy. Highly quotable. The beat between the revelation and the response is perfectly timed.

jokes.text: Ross's immediate verdict: 'That bitch.'
jokes.setup: Monica reveals Frannie betrayed Ross's Playboy secret to their mother
jokes.punchline: Ross's two-word verdict is delivered with the flat certainty of a man whose worst suspicions have been confirmed
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. Two words, no embellishment, maximum conviction. Ross saying 'That bitch.' in the same tone you'd use to say 'Of course.' is very funny. The pacing — a beat after the revelation — sells it completely.

jokes.text: The reveal that Monica wasn't invited because she slept with the groom: 'Stuart. I believe you know my husband. So it's really a question of who could you have possibly done.'
jokes.setup: Monica demands to know why she wasn't invited, insisting she couldn't have done anything wrong ('What could I have possibly done?')
jokes.punchline: Frannie introduces her husband Stuart — who Monica clearly recognizes — and Ross's reframe ('who' instead of 'what') lands the reveal with perfect precision
jokes.explanation: Best structural joke in the episode. The setup has been building for the entire wedding subplot — why was Monica not invited? The payoff recontextualizes Monica's indignant 'What could I have possibly done?' into a question with an embarrassing answer. Ross's grammar correction ('who' vs 'what') as the actual punchline delivery is elegant and precise. Near-perfect structure — the entire subplot pivots on one word. High earned vs. cheap because it's genuinely clever, not random. This is what a 9 on structure looks like.

jokes.text: David's Russian phrase turns out to mean 'Please clean my beakers': 'I don't get out of the lab much.'
jokes.setup: David says something in Russian to Phoebe, clearly intended to be romantic. Phoebe is moved.
jokes.punchline: The beautiful-sounding Russian turns out to be a lab instruction about cleaning beakers — with his sheepish 'I don't get out of the lab much' as the deflating tag
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The misdirect (romantic-sounding Russian → lab instruction) is well-executed, and 'I don't get out of the lab much' is a perfect character tag that makes it funnier and more sympathetic simultaneously. Pairs beautifully with the Lenin/Phoebe statue joke to establish David as a scientist so consumed by his work that romance and professional life have fused. High character integration because this joke only works for David specifically.

jokes.text: David's 'I do, though.' — implying 'I love you' without saying it, then Phoebe's 'I do too.'
jokes.setup: David says something he 'probably shouldn't' because he has to leave. Phoebe tells him not to say it.
jokes.punchline: He says it anyway — but only as 'I do, though' — the most economically romantic/comedic understatement possible. The unspoken declaration is more affecting than the words would be.
jokes.explanation: This sits at the border of comedy and genuine emotion — which is what makes it notable. The joke is the economy: 'I do, though' communicates everything while technically saying nothing. It's the comedic opposite of overexplanation. The structure (Phoebe says don't say it / he says it anyway but as a fragment) is tight. Scores high on economy and character integration because it's entirely in both characters' idiom.

jokes.text: Joey comforting Phoebe by offering: 'You could always visit him.' / Phoebe: 'Oh, right. Like they're gonna let me have a passport.'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to help Phoebe feel better about David leaving for Minsk
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's self-aware aside that she won't be allowed a passport — implying some unspecified past behavior that has flagged her as a risk to international travel — is a perfect Phoebe line
jokes.explanation: A stellar Phoebe joke. 'Like they're gonna let me have a passport' works on multiple levels: it's a perfect character reveal (what has she done??), it's delivered as a matter-of-fact grievance rather than a punchline, and it implies a whole world of Phoebe backstory we'll never fully know. Character integration is as high as it gets — this line belongs to no other character. Highly quotable and deeply rewatchable.

jokes.text: Phoebe asks Joey to achieve 'positronic distillation of subatomic particles' before David so he'll be forced to come back
jokes.setup: Joey asks if there's anything he can do to help Phoebe feel better about David leaving
jokes.punchline: Phoebe asks Joey — who is an actor with no scientific background — to beat a physicist at a highly specialized scientific achievement so David will have no reason to stay in Russia
jokes.explanation: Absurdist Phoebe logic at its finest — the solution she proposes is both impossibly specific ('positronic distillation of subatomic particles') and completely misassigned (asking Joey to do it). The gap between the problem and her proposed solution is characteristically Phoebe. Joey's earnest 'I could give it a shot' is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Joey's earnest response: 'I could give it a shot.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has asked Joey to achieve 'positronic distillation of subatomic particles'
jokes.punchline: Joey doesn't question it, ask what it means, or decline — he simply, earnestly offers to give it a shot, with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Five words that are entirely Joey. His complete willingness to attempt something he demonstrably has no capacity to do, with zero hesitation and maximum sincerity, is a perfect character beat. The economy score is near-maximum — he delivers all the character truth in five syllables. This is the comedic payoff to Phoebe's absurd request and it lands beautifully.

jokes.text: Chandler spots a piece of dropped cheesecake: 'Oh, look. There's a piece that doesn't have floor on it.' — visual of them eating dropped cheesecake off the hallway floor
jokes.setup: Rachel dropped her cheesecake earlier and they were separated. Now they're both in the hallway around the dropped cheesecake.
jokes.punchline: Chandler identifies a salvageable piece by its floor-to-cheesecake ratio — 'doesn't have floor on it' — implying they are now eating floor cheesecake, their moral degradation complete
jokes.explanation: Superb capper to the cheesecake storyline. 'Doesn't have floor on it' is a brilliantly specific phrase — the implied obverse is that MOST pieces do have floor on them. The arc of their moral collapse — from 'this is wrong' to 'we're living outside the law' to 'I'll take the piece without floor' — is complete. This is exactly how a storyline escalation should pay off. High originality for the specific phrasing.

jokes.text: Monica and Joey find Chandler and Rachel eating cheesecake off the hallway floor — their arrival and reaction
jokes.setup: Chandler and Rachel have been eating dropped cheesecake off the floor of their apartment hallway
jokes.punchline: Monica and Joey arrive and find them in this state — the entire cheesecake theft saga is exposed through visual discovery rather than confession
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff of the entire cheesecake storyline. Monica and Joey finding them hunched over floor cheesecake is the comedic culmination of the whole arc. What sells it is the implication — after all their moral agonizing, this is where they ended up. 'All right, what are we having?' is a perfect button.

jokes.text: Joey's immediate, unbothered reaction upon finding them eating floor cheesecake: 'All right, what are we having?'
jokes.setup: Monica and Joey have discovered Chandler and Rachel eating cheesecake off the hallway floor
jokes.punchline: Joey doesn't judge, doesn't express shock — he simply wants to know what food is available and joins in without a second thought
jokes.explanation: Best single-line joke in the episode. Five words that are purely, perfectly Joey. His complete absence of moral judgment, his immediate food-identification response, and the fact that he's apparently ready to join in eating floor cheesecake is character comedy at its peak. Character integration is as high as it can get — not a single other character in this ensemble would respond this way. The economy is maximum: 'All right, what are we having?' contains a complete comedic universe.

jokes.text: Callback: Aunt Millie kisses Ross on the lips again during the wrap-up. Ross again: 'Why? Why on the lips?'
jokes.setup: Ross is heading out after the wedding. Aunt Millie says goodbye.
jokes.punchline: She kisses him on the lips again — same gag, perfectly repeated — and Ross delivers the identical complaint with the same existential bewilderment, implying no lesson was learned by anyone
jokes.explanation: Textbook callback execution. The joke is funnier the second time because (a) we know what's coming and (b) the fact that Ross's protest did absolutely nothing makes his suffering funnier. The 'why?' repeated exactly as before signals learned helplessness. Good running gag payoff.

tmdb_overview: Phoebe gets upset with Joey when he blows off dinner with her for a date, however only a few days later she finds herself in the same situation but with their roles reversed. Meanwhile, Chandler and Rachel enjoy a cheesecake that gets delivered to their address by accident. They feel guilt-ridden at first, but it's just too delicious. Also, Ross and Monica attend a wedding reception of their cousin and find themselves in an awkward situation.
insight: Cheesecake obsession drives 52 jokes across 22 minutes—character comedy at its most repetitive.
